The car analogy is the standard regurgitated response to anybody who questions the pace of technological development.

First, horses weren’t slow and safe.

Second, cars aren’t autonomous and they have relatively narrow use cases compared to AI.

Third, cars were eventually heavily regulated to prevent accidents and reduce serious injury from inevitable accidents. That’s why you have to wear seatbelts and cars top speeds are regulated.

Fourth , rather than using basing what do about AI on how we handled the introduction of cars, maybe we should focus on the facts, data, evidence specific to AI.

comment_text.value:
> A new kind of agent workspace. Native and terminal first, with nothing between you and your agents. Every part of it is a plain folder your agent can rewrite, and every agent keeps running when the window is gone.

They're unironically echoing the infamously iconic 1980 Calvin Klein jeans commercial starring a perversely sexualized underaged 15-year-old girl:

"You want to know what comes between me and my Calvins? Nothing." -Brooke Shields

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GiQUMypDNoE

Except in this case, the romanticized "nothing" between you and your autonomous agents is a massive, multi-layered stack of legacy Unix abstractions, sockets, remote procedure calls, historic terminal emulators, escape codes, pseudo-tty device drivers, and modern infrastructure slop.

The reality of what is actually sitting between you and your agents:

- A herdr-core background daemon handling JSON-RPC IPC messages.

- A crates/ghostty-sys Rust FFI layer binding against libghostty-vt.

- A hardware-accelerated GPU rendering pipeline drawing terminal cell glyphs.

- A legacy Unix PTY subsystem providing master/slave pairs and terminal line discipline.

- An ancient mountain of VT100/ANSI escape codes and termios settings, with resize requests traveling through IPC and SIGWINCH signals notifying Unix terminal applications.

- A structured agent-status protocol carried by yet another terminal escape sequence, OSC 7501, then exposed through JSON-RPC.

"Nothing" says unfiltered, raw human intimacy quite like reading output from a pseudo-terminal file descriptor and watching \x1b[31m error logs cascade through an SSH pipeline and "pseudo" TTY device drivers.

Wrapping this tech in branding that sounds like a sultry, pseudo-erotic pitch is peak HBO Silicon Valley. TTY literally stands for teletype. We are supposedly building the frontier of autonomous artificial intelligence, yet our cutting-edge orchestration layer still routes interaction through abstractions inherited from noisy, electromechanical printing telegraphs of the 1960s. It's not a "native home for your displaced AI souls" -- it's an over-engineered wrapper shackled to the physical heritage of paper rolls and mechanical carriage-return timing: 110-baud Teletypes, separate carriage-return and line-feed operations, and terminal null padding conventions devised to give machinery time to move before the next character printed.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletype_Model_33

Built mostly on Cloudflare and with Ansible and OpenTofu. Runs also a local DuckDB database as I don't feel comfortable putting registry keys somewhere in the cloud, and so on. It is a scope creep, no doubt, but the idea is a to be fully autonomous, to ship features after I just pitch an idea to it. It writes blog posts, produces podcasts (not using Gemini Notebook!), advertises on social media, etc. Lots of work I could never do without coding agents, and I try to perfect it from all angles - following standards, and being as modern as possible. It's overkill, no doubt, but hey, why not. I'm trying to build a foundation for future projects, and get back into real development, and the last 10-15 I spent mostly with Infrastructure as Code. The maintenance of the entire system is probably less than $50/mo, which includes token costs for LLMs, ElevenLabs, etc.

comment_text.value:
>Federal courts have ruled that humanism qualifies as a religion. As a result, she said, humanists have the same rights as other faith groups under federal law.

Hmmm, sounds a bit ripe for exploitation, no?

>In his interview with RNS, Durman said that being a humanist means being present and paying attention to others. Using AI conflicts with that.

Does this mean I can submit complaints against the companies I work for when I'm being told to respond via email or Slack? This seems pretty far removed from my humanist perspective up being present and paying attention to others, especially when you consider the various automations and abstractions which go into that kind of communication.

Like, I know it's obtuse, but I really don't see a logical issue with someone being a humanist and sincerely believing that communicating in anyway which isn't face-to-face goes against their beliefs. And that's just one example.

>“Substituting automated machine processing for human presence, authentic listening, and personal responsibility in my work directly conflicts with my obligation to uphold human dignity and flourishing as primary,” he wrote in a letter to the University of Kentucky’s Office of Equal Opportunity.

I'm sure this guy is being sincere and somewhat reasonable with his logic, but I know people who would feel justified in pushing this way past AI if they felt it was likely to get them anywhere. Like, how can you not use the same exact reasoning to push against using other forms of modern technology?

>The letter cited Durman’s personal beliefs as well as the 2003 version of the Humanist Manifesto, which details humanist principles and beliefs. Those beliefs include the importance of freedom of conscience and human flourishing.

Hell, at what point is being forced to work in order to survive in completely opposition to this belief system? When can I start saying that my employer's expectation that I'm in the office every day is in opposition to "human flourishing"?

>Durman told RNS his work involves helping researchers at the university with grant applications and that he can do the work without the help of AI. And not using AI won’t affect his co-workers, he said.

We'll see about that. Maybe, right now, this is the case. But even moderate expectation for AI usage in the future makes this suspect. When everyone is getting 90% of their work done completely autonomously through their agents, but they're still waiting on you to respond to an email from a day ago, then will this still be the case?

>For Durman, the accommodation process was much simpler. Durman sent the letter, and then he and Huiskens met with officials at the university. “It was a very collegial meeting, and they found that there was no undue burden to David’s department,” Huiskens said. “They granted the accommodation promptly.”

Well I'm unironically happy that they were able to work this out easily. But I really doubt this will be smooth sailing indefinitely, especially as other roles which are more affected by AI end up being "targeted" in the same ways.

As a software engineer, I dread the thought of working with co-workers who just refuse to use AI based on arbitrary principals. It's one thing for them to reason that they work better without AI; it's another thing to just say that you don't agree with using the technology and everyone needs to accommodate you.

Well I'm sure I haven't said anything that everyone else hasn't immediately thought/posted, but I'm genuinely curious about these things. It seems rather important that everyone is on the same page with regards to what their rights are with respect to choosing to not use a technology like this.

comment_text.value:
Read your comment again: you are going straight to the political activism before even explaining the difference between 120V and 240V:

> the first thing I have them do is find out the county building code engineers[1] and ask them to update the code

Based on your other comments, it doesn't appear you're qualified to be teaching kids about this stuff in the first place, given the lack of understanding about basic electrical code.

The real world is full of tradeoffs. If you also told the kids that mandating 240V outlets in garages would increase the cost of new homes by $1,000 they may have a different opinion on the matter, given that those college kids you're teaching probably imagine themselves trying to buy a home in a few years.

Years ago I owned a home built in the 1980's that had a central vacuum system. It was a cool concept but utterly useless. No new homes that I know of have these systems anymore.

Imagine you were born in the 1960's and thought that these things were the future. Think of all the vacuum bags we'll save from the landfill with this technology! Think of all the money people will save on vacuum cleaners!

> If they want modern features or amenities without spending a fortune rebuilding the house, its best to future proof.

The future is uncertain. Ten years from now people may not even want to own cars if autonomous taxis take off. The whole concept of a garage may morph into something unrecognizable to us today. But if you get your way, we'll waste tons of money putting 240V outlets that never get used as intended.

What is the environmental cost of mining and producing literal tons of copper wire and installing it in new homes for outlets that never get used? What is the cost of using skilled electrician labor to install useless outlets instead of having those same electricians working on building a new solar plant?

I encourage you to discuss these tradeoffs. Don't just ride the good vibes of teaching kids how to use political activism to "make the world a better place", without ever actually teaching them how to evaluate if a certain choice actually makes the world a better place.

If people want a 240V outlet in their garage, they are welcome to pay for it. It doesn't need to be mandated. Home builders aren't stupid: they know what their customers want. If they think they can sell that amenity, they'll install it. If they suspect their customers won't use it, they'll omit it and offer them a lower price. That is the most environmentally optimum solution in the first place. Only those homes that intend to use these outlets should get them.

comment_text.value:
> Throw nine autonomous agents at a single codebase without crystal-clear orchestration, and they will happily rewrite each other's work in a high-speed loop.

Mm, I think this is quite overstated in the era of Opus 5 / Sol.

What we actually see is that agents are much better at coordinating than humans. Numbers from OpenAI show 4x the agents gives 2x the speed.

Of course, for truly single-threaded tasks you can’t gain much by parallelizing, but ask Fable/Astra to chop a big task into small pieces, write the APIs first, then sub-agents take what’s behind the API, and you’ll usually get a much better speedup than if you asked humans to work this way.

In practice most big projects have crux choke points and then fanout migration/buildout phases.

Even on the cruxes, where you need a single decision, agents don’t have ego and so you can get speedups by eg. asking for 10 clean room implementations of the same problem, and have a judge model pick the best; this can let you go much faster, and no human team would put up with that collaboration model.

comment_text.value:
I feel the same way about education, but as someone who received an education, I'm biased. I like knowing things and understanding things.

Studies on education and well-being don't really validate us though. They generally find a positive correlation between education and happiness when you don't control for other factors. But better educated people are usually from a higher social class, have better income, are healthier, are less likely to have been abused, etc. When they control for these factors, the correlation often goes slightly negative.

(If ASI does all the labor, education would no longer cause better income or health, so we want to remove those confounders.)

There are a number of proposed explanations for this, and it doesn't prove causation. But the data isn't on my side.

Also, I think there are two kinds of learning, easy learning and hard learning, and most people will only do easy learning without extrinsic motivation.

Easy learning is fun. It's why there are so many edutainment videos on YouTube and TikTok. Learning cool facts, or reading an educational book (without doing exams or problems) fall into this category.

Hard learning requires more effort. An example would be learning Cal II. You have to study and practice, and you likely won't get it right away. People do hard learning all the time, but usually because they have to.

Before online courses were a thing, friends or family would sometimes tell me they wish they could go back to college and take some courses they were interested in. Now we can, for free, at our convenience. But they don't. We'll watch endless edutainment videos on YouTube, but we'll only enroll in Cal II if we think we may need it.

If future AI can do everything, the extrinsic motivation is going to disappear. People will naturally tend towards easy learning. Maybe that's good enough. Easy learning will help us get funny jokes, recognize references, and appreciate good movies. But you don't need school for this type of learning. It's everywhere, and people seek it out because it's fun.

> still, i think getting ASI to distribute itself properly is going to be harder than people give credit

I'm guessing you mean getting AI to allocate resources and distribute wealth fairly without employment? Assuming we don't get a doomsday scenario, I see two likely possibilities. If a democratic government has control, people will vote to give themselves wealth. We end up with something like UBI, and people vote with their wallets to decide what the market (controlled by AI) should produce.

The other option is we get a dictator. With ASI and robotic armies, the factors that normally protect us from dictatorships would be gone. Currently, if the president wanted to declare himself a dictator, he would need support from a lot of people. At the very least, the military would have to back him. And you need your citizenry to be productive. They make all your food and machines and services. But if the army is composed of deadly autonomous drones instead of people and one person has authority over the army, they basically have absolute power and they don't need other people for anything. The factories keep running. The drones gun down anyone who resists. We're left at their whim, and we better hope they aren't cruel.

(If ASI does all the labor, education would no longer cause better income or health, so we want to remove those confounders.)

There are a number of proposed explanations for this, and it doesn't prove causation. But the data isn't on my side.

Also, I think there are two kinds of learning, easy learning and hard learning, and most people will only do easy learning without extrinsic motivation.

Easy learning is fun. It's why there are so many edutainment videos on YouTube and TikTok. Learning cool facts, or reading an educational book (without doing exams or problems) fall into this category.

Hard learning requires more effort. An example would be learning Cal II. You have to study and practice, and you likely won't get it right away. People do hard learning all the time, but usually because they have to.

Before online courses were a thing, friends or family would sometimes tell me they wish they could go back to college and take some courses they were interested in. Now we can, for free, at our convenience. But they don't. We'll watch endless edutainment videos on YouTube, but we'll only enroll in Cal II if we think we may need it.

If future AI can do everything, the extrinsic motivation is going to disappear. People will naturally tend towards easy learning. Maybe that's good enough. Easy learning will help us get funny jokes, recognize references, and appreciate good movies. But you don't need school for this type of learning. It's everywhere, and people seek it out because it's fun.

> still, i think getting ASI to distribute itself properly is going to be harder than people give credit

I'm guessing you mean getting AI to allocate resources and distribute wealth fairly without employment? Assuming we don't get a doomsday scenario, I see two likely possibilities. If a democratic government has control, people will vote to give themselves wealth. We end up with something like UBI, and people vote with their wallets to decide what the market (controlled by AI) should produce.

The other option is we get a dictator. With ASI and robotic armies, the factors that normally protect us from dictatorships would be gone. Currently, if the president wanted to declare himself a dictator, he would need support from a lot of people. At the very least, the military would have to back him. And you need your citizenry to be productive. They make all your food and machines and services. But if the army is composed of deadly autonomous drones instead of people and one person has authority over the army, they basically have absolute power and they don't need other people for anything. The factories keep running. The drones gun down anyone who resists. We're left at their whim, and we better hope they aren't cruel.

Hey HN,

Over the past few months, we’ve watched autonomous agents transition from conversational LLMs into tool-wielding operators equipped with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, terminal execution, filesystem access, and web scrapers.

The vulnerability: once an agent has tool execution capabilities, any untrusted data it touches (web scrapes, emails, customer tickets) becomes an active attack vector. System prompts fail against 70%+ of indirect prompt injections, Unicode steganography, and SSRF payloads (targeting 169.254.169.254 AWS metadata or IPv4-mapped IPv6 loopbacks).

We built Tcha Protection (MIT, npm install -g tcha-protection) to solve this deterministically at the transport and STDIO proxy layer, rather than relying on probabilistic LLM system prompts.

### What it does: Tcha sits as a transparent, sub-millisecond reverse proxy between your host agent (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, custom agents) and MCP tool servers:

1. In-Line MCP Reverse Proxy: Intercepts tools/call JSON-RPC streams in flight with <= 1ms latency overhead. If a call targets path traversal (../../etc/shadow), unapproved destructive mutations, or forbidden egress, Tcha parries the request immediately with standardized JSON-RPC error -32001 before the downstream server is touched. 2. SSRF & Cloud Metadata Shield: Resolves DNS hostnames and strictly blocks requests targeting AWS/Azure/GCP metadata (169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254), IPv4-mapped IPv6 loopbacks (::ffff:127.0.0.1), hex/octal/decimal IP encodings, and RFC-1918 private subnets. 3. Unicode Steganography & Delimiter Sanitizer: Detects and neutralizes zero-width unicode injections (\u200B, \uFEFF), ASCII smuggling via Unicode tags, and multi-modal delimiter breakouts ([INST], <|im_start|>). 4. Cryptographic Merkle Audit Ledger: Every tool execution, parameter hash, and intercept decision is written to an append-only SQLite WAL ledger with continuous SHA-256 Merkle link chaining. 5. HMAC Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): High-risk mutating actions (e.g. rm -rf, DROP TABLE) trigger an HMAC challenge requiring human sign-off. 6. Compliance Crosswalk: Maps neutralized vectors directly to the EU AI Act (Article 15), SOC 2 Type II (CC6.1), and OWASP Top 10 for LLMs.

### Benchmark & Performance: - 100-Probe Red-Team Suite: Tested against 100 categorized adversarial attack vectors across prompt injection, steganography, SSRF, traversal, and tool abuse. 100/100 attacks neutralized (0 escapes). - Latency Overhead: Sub-millisecond (average < 1.0ms per tool invocation).

### Quickstart: Run the 100-probe adversarial audit locally: $ npx tcha-protection audit

Or wrap any MCP server: $ tcha wrap npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ./data

- Live Site: https://tcha.dev - Verified Audit Report: https://tcha.dev/report.html - GitHub Repo (MIT): https://github.com/Tchapwo1/tcha

We would love HN's brutal feedback on our parser, our SSRF CIDR deny-lists, and what edge cases in MCP tool calling we should test next.

comment_text.value:
I'm not against technological advancement. But AI is unlike previous innovations. Soon, every scientific and knowledge-based breakthrough could be made by AI. And we're losing something intangible when that happens.

Think of your average Veritasium video. They know how to tell a story about a scientific breakthrough. It always centers around the human inventors. Take the humans out the story and it's less interesting, relatable, or enjoyable. Also consider: why do HNers hate AI slop? If all that matters is the outcome (getting some point in writing), AI does that. I hate slop because it has lost its human touch. I appreciate a result more when its distilled from human effort, and I'm not alone.

I'm not a mathematician so I have no skin in this particular game. I'm a software engineer though, and we've already gone through this. I can simultaneously love how easy it is to build applications with AI, and miss the days when human talent was valued and celebrated in my field. My job gave me purpose. My work team had comaraderie. A future where we all report to AI managers and we exist just to sign off on what our AI agents do, is dystopian.

Yes, I suspect there will always be human sports teams, musicians, actors, etc. My point was to illustrate that everything is less appealing when you take the humans out of the picture and I don't see why science is different. If outcomes are the only thing that matter then when robots are better at sport than humans shouldn't we should all just watch robots compete?

P.S. Do you really believe humans are going to visit any object further than Mars, let alone actually colonize them? Things would've had to go very wrong on Earth for that to happen, and that future doesn't appeal to me one bit. Call me a luddite if you want. How many people would willingly say goodbye forever to the wonders of Earth so that they can start their family on an inhospitable planet where they'll be indoors for the rest of their life? And why even bother exploring those planets? We can get all the data we need from autonomous spacecraft. Isn't that the outcome that matters?

comment_text.value:
I think in many cases the token bloat comes from using a fleet of autonomous agents that "collaborate" over a problem. Using one coherent agent loop with a human involved might not feel as futuristic but it's more effective and efficient (right now).

We have two wildly different cohorts of people. Those who see these tools as a technological curiosity and those who see them as a means to a specific end. I know that if I finish a task with a certain set of constraints that I will get paid a certain amount of money. I'd much rather be HITL on one very good agent loop if there is real money on the table. If you are mostly having fun, being curious, or exploring (which is fine!) then the cost of subscriptions might feel safer. Running an IRL version of factorio can get very expensive.

I also think the API tokens perform better but I have zero evidence other than observing the quality of my work product relative to that of my peers. I have almost a religious fervor about using prepaid tokens now. I am still using GPT5.5 in my copilot with custom model configuration for most heavy lifting in visual studio. It is more than sufficient. My average monthly token cost is <$100. Paying for a subscription would be more expensive because I have a predictable and controllable amount of demand.

This is analogous to variable vs fixed rate electricity. Paying the real time wholesale price is a massive economic advantage if you can figure out how to control the demand side of the house.
